preamble: Loss of glottalization and affrication: Proto-Semitic emphatic *ṣ, reconstructed as the ejective affricate *tsʼ, ends up as plain [s]. In Akkadian this happens directly but rarely under Geers's law, since ṣ is the most stable emphatic and yields only exceptionally (siāqu 'be narrow', from a root with lateral *ṣ́ that had merged with ṣ); Akkadian s may itself still have been [ts] at the time. Maltese and Cypriot Maronite Arabic reach s in two steps, through pharyngealized sˤ (*tsʼ > sˤ > s); each step is filed separately. A direct, regular case is Athabaskan: stem-final *tsʼ became s in Hupa, Wailaki and Jicarilla (Navajo has voiced z/ʒ).

examples.from: Pre-Akkadian *ṣ (< Proto-Semitic *ṣ́) in the root ṣ-y-q 'be narrow'
examples.note: Proto-Semitic lateral *ṣ́ had already merged with *ṣ in Akkadian; the sibilant then loses emphasis next to the kept q. Arabic ḍāqa 'be narrow', Hebrew ṣûq 'constrain, press upon'. Described as 'very rare' (Shaffer 2007).
